title: Stewardship, Work and Money
summary: Living as God's stewards: the meaning of work, biblical teaching on money, giving and tithing, debt and saving, and a fair look at prosperity teaching.
description: Everything we have belongs to God. This course teaches the principle of stewardship, the dignity and purpose of work, what the Bible says about wealth, contentment and greed, giving and the tithing debate, wise budgeting, saving and debt, and how to evaluate prosperity teaching with Scripture.
objectives: Explain stewardship as a foundation for life and money
Teach a biblical view of work and vocation
Explain Scripture's teaching on wealth, poverty and contentment
Present the views on tithing and principles of generous giving
Evaluate prosperity teaching fairly from Scripture
outcomes: Apply the parable of the talents to daily life
Work with integrity as service to Christ
Make a simple budget and debt plan
Explain the tithing debate and New Testament giving principles
Distinguish biblical blessing from prosperity-gospel claims

modules.title: Everything Belongs to God
modules.intro: Stewardship means managing what belongs to someone else. This week we see that God owns all and entrusts it to us.

lessons.title: The earth is the LORD's
lessons.body:
"The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein" (Psalm 24:1). "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD" (Haggai 2:8).

We are **stewards**, not owners: managers of God's property. "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2).

Stewardship covers all of life: time (Ephesians 5:16), body (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), gifts (1 Peter 4:10), money, relationships and creation itself (Genesis 2:15). The question is not "How much of my money should I give God?" but "How should I use God's money?"

lessons.title: The parable of the talents
lessons.body:
In Matthew 25:14-30 a master entrusts talents to three servants "every man according to his several ability". Two trade and double their talents; the master says, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things."

The third buries his talent out of fear and is condemned as "wicked and slothful".

Lessons: God gives different amounts; He expects faithful use, not equal results; laziness and fear are not neutral; and there will be an accounting.

lessons.title: Caring for creation
lessons.body:
God put man in the garden "to dress it and to keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Dominion (Genesis 1:28) means responsible rule as God's representatives, not destruction.

God cares for animals (Psalm 104:14; Jonah 4:11), gave rest to the land (Leviticus 25:4), and will renew creation (Romans 8:21).

Practical stewardship includes avoiding waste, disposing of refuse properly, not polluting rivers, planting trees, and caring for animals. Poor stewardship of land and water harms the poor most.

terms.def: Faithfully managing what belongs to God for His purposes.
A manager entrusted with another's property.
In Jesus' parable, a large sum of money entrusted to a servant.
Reliable, diligent use of what God entrusts.
Humanity's responsible rule over creation as God's representatives.
The certainty that each will give account of their stewardship (Romans 14:12).

texts.teaches: The earth is the LORD's and all its fulness.
Stewards must be found faithful.
Well done, good and faithful servant.
He that is faithful in least is faithful also in much.
God put man in the garden to dress it and keep it.

summary: God owns everything; we are stewards.
Stewardship covers time, body, gifts, money and creation.
God expects faithful use of what He gives, and will call us to account.
Caring for creation is part of stewardship.

questions.q: Why was the third servant condemned?
options: He buried his talent out of fear and laziness

questions.q: Why did God put man in the garden?
options: To dress it and keep it

modules.title: The Dignity of Work
modules.intro: Work is not a curse but a calling. This week we study a biblical view of work.

lessons.title: Work before the fall
lessons.body:
God Himself works: He created for six days and rested (Genesis 2:2). Man was given work before sin entered (Genesis 2:15). Work is part of being made in God's image.

After the fall work became toilsome: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread" (Genesis 3:19). But work itself remains good.

Jesus worked as a carpenter (Mark 6:3); Paul made tents (Acts 18:3). Every honest job, whether trading, farming, teaching, driving, nursing or cleaning, can glorify God. There is no split between 'sacred' ministry and 'secular' work.

lessons.title: Working as unto the Lord
lessons.body:
"And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men... for ye serve the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:23-24). Even slaves were told to work faithfully "not with eyeservice, as menpleasers" (3:22).

Christian workers should be diligent (Proverbs 22:29), honest, punctual and respectful. Christian employers must pay fair wages on time: "the hire of the labourers... kept back by fraud, crieth" (James 5:4), and treat workers justly (Colossians 4:1).

Work also provides for family (1 Timothy 5:8) and enables giving: "let him labour... that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Ephesians 4:28).

lessons.title: Laziness, rest and unemployment
lessons.body:
Scripture condemns laziness: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Proverbs 6:6). "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

But God also commands rest. The sabbath principle guards against overwork and greed (Exodus 20:8-11; Mark 2:27). Burnout is not holiness: "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows" (Psalm 127:2).

Unemployment is a hard trial, not a sign of God's rejection. Believers should seek work diligently, learn skills, start small enterprises, and the church should help with training, connections and support.

terms.def: God's calling to serve Him and others through our work and roles.
The false idea that only church work pleases God.
Working only when watched, to please people.
A lazy person, warned in Proverbs.
God's pattern of regular rest from work.
Just and timely pay for work done (James 5:4).

texts.teaches: Whatever you do, do it heartily as to the Lord.
A man diligent in business shall stand before kings.
Wages kept back by fraud cry out to God.
Go to the ant, thou sluggard, and be wise.
It is vain to rise early and sit up late eating the bread of sorrows.

summary: Work was given before the fall and is part of bearing God's image.
All honest work can be done as service to Christ.
Workers must be diligent; employers must pay fairly.
Avoid laziness and overwork; support the unemployed.

questions.q: When was work given to man?

modules.title: Money, Contentment and Prosperity
modules.intro: Money is a tool, not a god. This week we study wealth, greed, contentment and prosperity teaching.

lessons.title: Wealth and its dangers
lessons.body:
Wealth can be a blessing from God (Deuteronomy 8:18; Proverbs 10:22). Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly.

But riches are dangerous. "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith" (1 Timothy 6:10). Jesus warned, "Ye cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24) and "a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luke 12:15).

The rich are to be "rich in good works, ready to distribute" (1 Timothy 6:17-19). God cares deeply for the poor (Proverbs 19:17) and condemns oppression.

lessons.title: Contentment
lessons.body:
"But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Timothy 6:6-7).

Paul learned contentment in both plenty and want: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Philippians 4:11-13). Note that 4:13 is about contentment, not a promise of success in everything.

Contentment frees us from envy, from comparing ourselves on social media, and from dishonest gain. "Let your conversation be without covetousness... for he hath said, I will never leave thee" (Hebrews 13:5).

lessons.title: Evaluating prosperity teaching
lessons.body:
The **prosperity gospel** teaches that God always wills believers to be wealthy and healthy, and that faith, positive confession and giving (often to the preacher) guarantee material increase.

Its appeal includes truths: God does bless, cares about our needs, and rewards generosity (2 Corinthians 9:6-8).

But Scripture corrects it:

- Jesus became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9) and promised trouble in the world (John 16:33).
- Paul knew hunger and need (2 Corinthians 11:27).
- Godliness is not "a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5).
- Selling blessings for money is condemned (Acts 8:20).

The true riches are in Christ (Ephesians 1:3).

terms.def: Wealth treated as a master or god (Matthew 6:24).
Greedy desire for more, especially for what belongs to others.
Peaceful satisfaction in God whatever one's circumstances.
Teaching that faith and giving guarantee wealth and health.
The prosperity teaching that speaking words of faith creates reality.
Paul's charge to wealthy believers (1 Timothy 6:18).

texts.teaches: The love of money is the root of all evil.
You cannot serve God and mammon.
Paul learned to be content in every state.
Be without covetousness; God will never leave you.
Christ became poor that we might be rich.

summary: Wealth can be a blessing, but the love of money is dangerous.
Godliness with contentment is great gain.
Philippians 4:13 is about contentment in all circumstances.
Prosperity teaching contains some truths but distorts the gospel.

questions.q: What is the root of all evil, according to 1 Timothy 6:10?
Which text corrects the idea that godliness is a means of gain?

modules.title: Giving, Budgeting and Debt
modules.intro: This week we study generous giving, the tithing debate, and practical money management.

lessons.title: Generous giving and the tithe
lessons.body:
Christians agree that giving should be **regular** (1 Corinthians 16:2), **proportionate** ("as God hath prospered him"), **cheerful** (2 Corinthians 9:7), **sacrificial** like the widow's mite (Mark 12:41-44), and **for gospel work and the poor** (Galatians 6:6; 2:10).

On the **tithe** (a tenth), views differ:

- Many churches, including many Pentecostal and Baptist churches, teach the tithe as a continuing standard, citing Abraham before the law (Genesis 14:20), Malachi 3:10 and Jesus' affirmation (Matthew 23:23).
- Others teach the tithe was part of the Mosaic law and that New Testament giving is freewill and generous, often more than a tenth.

Both reject giving under pressure, manipulation or as a purchase of blessing.

lessons.title: Budgeting and saving
lessons.body:
"For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?" (Luke 14:28). A budget is simply planning how to use God's money.

A simple plan:

1. **Give** first (Proverbs 3:9).
2. **Provide** for necessities: food, rent, transport, school fees.
3. **Save** for emergencies and the future, like the ant (Proverbs 6:8) and Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 41:34-36).
4. **Spend** the rest wisely.

Track income and spending for a month. Avoid 'get-rich-quick' schemes and Ponzi schemes: "he that hasteth to be rich shall not be innocent" (Proverbs 28:20).

lessons.title: Debt and financial integrity
lessons.body:
Scripture does not forbid all borrowing, but warns: "the borrower is servant to the lender" (Proverbs 22:7). "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another" (Romans 13:8) at least means paying debts as agreed: "The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again" (Psalm 37:21).

Guidelines: avoid debt for consumption and show; be cautious about loan apps with crushing interest; do not stand surety rashly (Proverbs 22:26-27); repay debts faithfully; never borrow without a plan to repay.

Financial integrity also means paying taxes (Romans 13:7), keeping honest records, and refusing fraud. Money handled faithfully is a powerful witness.

terms.def: A tenth of one's income given to God.
A gift given voluntarily beyond what is required.
Giving in proportion to how God has prospered us (1 Corinthians 16:2).
A plan for using income on giving, needs, saving and spending.
Guaranteeing another's debt, which Proverbs warns against.
A fraud paying earlier investors with money from new ones, promising quick riches.

texts.teaches: God loves a cheerful giver.
Bring all the tithes into the storehouse.
Count the cost before you build.
The borrower is servant to the lender.
The wicked borrows and does not pay back.

summary: Giving should be regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial.
Christians differ on whether the tithe is binding today; all reject manipulation.
Budget: give, provide, save and spend wisely; avoid get-rich-quick schemes.
Borrow cautiously, repay faithfully and pay taxes honestly.

What do both views on tithing reject?
options: Giving under pressure or to buy blessing

short.model: Faithfully managing what belongs to God, since He owns everything and we are His stewards.

short.q: What does the parable of the talents teach?
short.model: God entrusts different amounts and expects faithful use; fearful laziness is condemned and there will be an accounting.

short.q: Why is all honest work valuable to God?
short.model: Work was given before the fall as part of God's image; all honest work can be done heartily for Christ, as Jesus the carpenter showed.
It rightly says God blesses and rewards generosity, but distorts the gospel by promising wealth; Christ became poor, Paul suffered need, and godliness is not a means of gain.

short.q: Summarise the two views of tithing.
short.model: Some teach the tithe as a continuing standard (Abraham, Malachi 3:10); others see it as Mosaic law, with New Testament giving freewill and generous.

short.q: Give three biblical principles about debt.
short.model: The borrower is servant to the lender, debts must be repaid, and we should avoid rash surety and borrowing without a plan.

assignments.title: A stewardship plan
assignments.prompt: Track your income and spending for two weeks. Then write a stewardship plan using the give-provide-save-spend pattern, with biblical reasons from the course for each part and one area you will change.

assignments.title: Prosperity and the gospel
assignments.prompt: Evaluate a sermon, song or advert you have encountered that promises wealth through faith or giving. Identify what is true in it and what is unbiblical, using at least five passages from this course.
